anatomy.lede: Out of its burrow, the zebra mantis shrimp is a long, boldly banded animal with stalked eyes and a pair of folded hunting limbs held beneath its head like a praying mantis.

hotspots.label: Stalked eyes
hotspots.text: The eyes sit on movable stalks. Before an attack, they are often the only part of the animal showing above the burrow.

hotspots.label: Raptorial claw
hotspots.text: The hunting limbs are modified second maxillipeds. In spearers like this one, the last segment is unfolded, elongated and lined with sharp spines for snagging fish.

hotspots.label: Banded body
hotspots.text: Dark and pale bands run across the long, segmented body, giving the animal its common name.

senses.lede: Mantis shrimps have some of the most complex eyes of any animal. Their young start life with far simpler ones.

senses.name: Colour vision
senses.text: Adult mantis shrimps have photoreceptors that detect up to 12 different colours, almost four times as many types as most animals. Why they need so many is still not understood.

senses.name: Larval eyes
senses.text: Zebra mantis shrimp larvae caught at Lizard Island had eyes with a single type of colour receptor, like other plankton. The complex adult eye is grown anew at metamorphosis.

body.lede: The zebra mantis shrimp carries the same strike machinery as its famous hammer-wielding relatives, but uses it differently.

systems.title: A spring it rarely uses
systems.text: Scans and dissections showed that it has the spring-and-latch structures other mantis shrimps use for spring-loaded strikes. Yet high-speed films suggest that it does not consistently use them.

systems.title: Reach over force
systems.text: Smashers need force to break shells, but a spearer needs reach to snatch fast prey. Its strikes are slower and longer than a smasher's, but match those of other predators of fast-moving prey.

systems.title: Bigger claws for males
systems.text: Males and females are similar in overall size, but males have larger raptorial claws.

genome.lede: No reference genome exists yet, but a 2025 'genome survey' estimated the size of the zebra mantis shrimp's DNA — and it is enormous.

findings.title: A giant genome
findings.text: Genome size was estimated at about 12.7 billion base pairs, the largest of the three mantis shrimps surveyed. More than 83% of the DNA in these species is repetitive.

findings.title: A missing mitochondrial gene
findings.text: Its mitochondrial genome is 16,204 base pairs long and lacks the ATP8 gene, as does that of the peacock mantis shrimp.

findings.title: An early branch
findings.text: Family trees built from several types of genetic data place the zebra mantis shrimp near the base of the group, though relationships among mantis shrimps remain disputed.

mind.lede: Watching mantis shrimps in the wild showed that they behave very differently from animals filmed in aquarium tanks.

studies.title: Variable strikes in the wild
studies.text: In the field, zebra mantis shrimps struck at passing prey with both longer and shorter strikes than those recorded in the laboratory.

studies.title: Sharing a burrow
studies.text: Pairs are socially monogamous and share a burrow. Building such a burrow is costly, and finding a mate is risky, which may explain why pairs stay together.

survival.lede: For a large but soft-bodied ambusher, the burrow is everything: a hiding place, a hunting blind and a home for two.

tactics.title: Hidden in the sand
tactics.text: It hides in a sandy burrow with only its eyes showing, then lunges out to seize prey with both claws.

tactics.title: Night hunting
tactics.text: In the field it ambushed evasive prey mainly at night.

threats.title: Fishing
threats.text: There is a small artisanal fishery for this species.

life.lede: Like other mantis shrimps, the zebra mantis shrimp begins life drifting in the plankton before settling into a burrow.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female looks after the eggs.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Late-stage larvae have been caught at the sea surface at night. Mantis shrimp larvae can pass through up to 11 drifting stages, depending on the species.

stages.name: Metamorphosis
stages.text: In the final hours of larval life, a completely new adult retina grows beside the old larval eye, which is later pushed aside and reabsorbed.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults live in sandy burrows, usually as a male–female pair.
